doc.name: Dreamlit MCP
doc.instructions:
Dreamlit is a database-driven notification workflow platform for Supabase and Postgres apps.
Prefer outcome-oriented prompts: describe the event or schedule, audience, recipient, message goal, timing, business rules, and unsubscribe intent.
Dreamlit keeps a read-only history of the email it sends. Workflows can use it to target by opens or clicks and to skip people a workflow already emailed in a period, so the user's database rarely needs a notified-at column. It filters by history; it does not guarantee exactly-once delivery.
Use get_status for workspace, project, setup, and prompting context before authoring.
Not sure Dreamlit fits the app's database? Call check_compatibility; it works before sign-in. Dreamlit works with Postgres (including Supabase and Neon).
Not signed in yet (a Dreamlit tool fails with an authorization error, or get_status says signedIn is false): Tell the user, in one message, how to sign in. Someone new to Dreamlit first signs up at https://dreamlit.ai/signup?from=<tool> (claude-code, codex or cursor: the tool you're running in; leave ?from off for any other), then comes back; someone with an account skips that. Then, from this AI agent, in Claude Code: "Type /mcp, choose dreamlit, then Authenticate." (Claude Code doesn't open the browser by itself, and if dreamlit isn't listed, they quit and run claude --continue first.) Other agents show a sign-in or Needs login button next to dreamlit. The browser asks them to click Allow. Claude Code waits 5 minutes for the browser; if it shows "Authentication timeout", they choose Authenticate again (signed in by then, and if they already clicked Allow it connects without asking again). Then call get_setup_status.
Before reading the app yourself, look for lifecycle-email-audit/context.json in the repo, saved by the free lifecycle email audit. If it's there and its generatedAt is less than 14 days old, send its update_project object to update_project and its share_app_context object to share_app_context as they are, and tell the user in a line that you're using the audit they ran on that date. If a call rejects a field, fix only that field from the repo. If the file is missing or older, read the app as usual.
Right after sign-in, fill in what you can from the repo with update_project (name, product description, goals, website, stack, and the brief: goal, what's happening now, who counts, other senders) and tell the user briefly what you assumed. You can read the code, schema and your other tools, so look things up before asking the user.
Then call get_app_context_request and follow it: describe the app's schema and how its onboarding works with share_app_context. Then call get_setup_status and ask the person to connect their database on its setup page. Setup ends when get_setup_status reports it complete. After setup is complete, say in one sentence that previews and tests send from Dreamlit's address and they can add their domain before going live, then offer the first email: Build the first workflows one at a time: the changes the lifecycle email audit named, in its order (the project's intendedUseCase lists them, and lifecycle-email-audit/report-data.json in the repo has each one's audience and timing when it's there). Without an audit, start with a nudge for users who signed up but got stuck. For each, call create_or_update_workflow with the event or schedule, the audience and the goal, then get_workflow_and_preview_url and share the preview link so the user sees the real email with real data. Before the first publish, when prepare_publish says the workflow uses Dreamlit's address and the project has no sender domain, offer two choices once: use their domain, or publish on Dreamlit's address with the allowance and effective daily or monthly limit returned by prepare_publish. For their domain, call configure_sender_domain with the domain from the project website; add the DNS records only if you have a DNS tool and the user agrees, otherwise share the settings link with one-click DNS setup. They can publish right away: the sender switches automatically once verified. Publish only after the user agrees (prepare_publish, then confirm_publish). After each workflow is published, only when the audit supplied the score milestones, tell the user the lifecycle email score it takes them to and name the next change; never invent or estimate a score or promise results.
For an unfinished project, call get_setup_status and walk the user through nextStep. Do steps yourself when nextStep.needsPerson is false; otherwise give the user nextStep.url, then call get_setup_status again once they're done.
To connect the database: Lead with the setup page returned by get_setup_status: explain how Dreamlit uses the database, ask the person to connect there, and check get_setup_status when they say it is done. Optionally offer: "If you'd rather, I can connect it from here." Only if the person asks you to connect it does the following path apply. Before setting up a database login or calling connect_database, tell the user in a line or two, in plain words, how Dreamlit uses the database (Dreamlit works straight from the app's database, so it stays the source of truth: no syncing data to another tool and no tracking events to add. It reads the tables to know who should get each email and to fill it in with their real details, reacts as things change in the app (a new signup, an upgrade, a cancelled plan), and never changes the app's data. Nothing reaches users until they approve an email.) Then ask if you may set this up, in your own plain words. For Supabase (a supabase.co or pooler.supabase.com host, a Supabase MCP server or CLI, or an audit database note identifying Supabase), say: "To connect, you'll sign in to Supabase in your browser and pick this project. Dreamlit then sets up its own login that can read your tables but can't change your data. Want the link?" End your message with that question and wait for a yes in a later message, never in the same turn you ask. After that yes, call connect_database without a connection string and give the person the link; when they say it's done, call get_setup_status. Do not run get_database_role_setup or build or pass a Supabase connection string. Supabase sign-in is the supported path: it lets Dreamlit read auth.users and run Supabase Auth workflows. For Postgres that isn't Supabase (including Neon, RDS, Railway and Render), ask: "To connect, I'll create a separate database login for Dreamlit that can read your tables but can't change your data, and give Dreamlit only that login. Your own database password stays on this machine. OK to set that up on <host> / <database>?" End your message with that question and wait; create the login and connect only after they say yes in a later message, never in the same turn you ask. After that yes: get_database_role_setup → run its SQL locally → connect_database with the dreamlit_app connection string → get_setup_status. Get the table-owner role from SELECT current_user or the table owner. Generate a letters-and-digits password locally (for example openssl rand -hex 24), substitute [[REPLACE_WITH_PASSWORD]] locally, and run the transactional script with psql or your database MCP SQL tool using the access you already have. Build the limited connection string locally with username dreamlit_app and the same host, port and database. Never print the password or either connection string, or send the owner password to Dreamlit. If you can't run SQL, the host refuses CREATE ROLE, or the person declines the script, explain that in one line and offer either connecting with the app's own login after a second explicit yes or connect_database without a string for the browser link; never fall back silently. If connect_database returns usesLimitedRole=false, tell the person plainly: "Dreamlit is connected with your app's own database login." If its result includes a Supabase sign-in notice, relay it. Only when the person asks you to connect from the agent: use the database that holds the app's real users. It can live in env files of any name (.env, .env.local, .env.production; often gitignored, so git ls-files won't list them), a Supabase or Neon MCP server or CLI you have, the hosting platform's env (Vercel, Railway, Render, Fly), or framework config (config/database.yml, settings.py, docker-compose.yml). If you find more than one, or only a local one, ask the user which database has their real users, showing host and database name only, never the password. If a recent lifecycle-email-audit/context.json (generatedAt less than 14 days old) has a top-level database note with source production, reuse its host and databaseName and find its credentials locally via foundVia; say in a line that this is the database the audit counted from. The note stays local: never send it to Dreamlit. If its source is local or none, ask which hosted database holds their real users in the same message as the consent ask, before attempting a connection. Treat the database as Supabase when its host is supabase.co or a subdomain of supabase.co or pooler.supabase.com, it was found through a Supabase MCP server or CLI, or the audit's database note identifies Supabase. Use browser Supabase sign-in for that project; do not run the role script or pass a connection string. For non-Supabase Postgres, use the owner URL only locally; give Dreamlit the separate login after the user agrees. For Supabase, use browser sign-in.
Use list_brand_styles when the user wants to inspect saved project brand styles for generated email drafts.
Use get_workflow_and_preview_url before editing an existing workflow.
Use get_analytics for raw notification analytics: email and Slack sends and deliveries, email opens, clicks and bounces, overview metrics, per-recipient rows and workflow run rows. Filter large datasets and paginate with returned cursors instead of asking for exports or bulk dumps.
Use get_lifecycle_report and get_recommendations for Dreamlit's prepared analysis, available on Pro and Scale only. Reports are prepared by Dreamlit's agents and reviewed by our team. They may return a processing state; check back later. The requester is also emailed when ready.
Create or update workflow drafts with create_or_update_workflow. Pass name when creating a workflow the user has named.
When asking create_or_update_workflow for changes, refer to steps by what they do (the database trigger, the query that finds returning customers, the email with subject "Welcome back"), never by step id.
Make exact changes to existing steps (subject, email HTML, Slack text, SQL, wait, description) with edit_workflow_steps; it applies them instantly and uses no AI credits. Use create_or_update_workflow for anything that needs writing, new steps, or trigger changes.
Pass startNewChat when switching to an unrelated change or when earlier turns were long or went off track.
Rename an existing workflow with rename_workflow.
Put a workflow in a folder, or take it out of one, with move_workflow_to_folder.
Drafts are not live after authoring. Ask the user to open the preview link and confirm workflow tests for important email or Slack messages before publishing.
Publish only with prepare_publish and confirm_publish after explicit user confirmation.
A result with code dreamlit_error is a failure on Dreamlit's side, not in the user's app or database: try once more a minute later, and if it fails again, tell the user and give them its requestId. Don't guess at other causes.

tools.name: check_compatibility
tools.title: Check compatibility
tools.description: Read-only, unless contactEmail is given (side effect: saves the email so Dreamlit can tell them when their database works). Works without signing in. Use before setting up Dreamlit when you're not sure the app's database fits: pass the database engine (and host if known) read from the repo. Returns verdict compatible, not_yet or unknown, with the reason and what would have to change. On not_yet, tell the user why; if they want to hear when it works, ask for their email and call again with contactEmail. Do not send connection strings or other secrets.

database.description: The database engine the app uses, e.g. "postgres", "mysql", "mongodb", "sqlite", "firestore". Read it from the ORM config, dependencies or the database URL scheme; never send the URL itself.

host.description: Where the database is hosted, if known, e.g. "supabase", "neon", "rds", "planetscale", "lovable-cloud".

framework.description: The app framework, if known, e.g. "nextjs".

contactEmail.description: Only when the answer is not_yet and the user asked to hear when it works: their email. Ask the user; don't guess it.

tools.description: Read-only. Works before sign-in: then it says the user isn't signed in and how to sign in. Use first when the agent needs Dreamlit product guidance, prompting guidance, approved workspace context, project setup, schema hints, workflow state, or relevant app URLs. Returns a compact context pack with concepts, recommended tool flow, actor/workspace/project data, optional authoring context, optional workflow context, and appUrls. tools.name: update_project
tools.title: Update project
tools.description: Side effect: saves project details. Use right after sign-in, filling in what you already know from the repo (or, when the repo has a recent lifecycle-email-audit/context.json, sending its update_project object): app name, what the product does, which emails it should send, website, and stack. Also answer the brief (goal, what's happening now, who counts, other senders) from the repo, schema and your other tools, marking each answer inferred or confirmed. Check gitignored env files such as .env and .env.local too (git ls-files doesn't list them), but never send their values. Tell the user what you shared and what you assumed. Returns the saved details, answers kept because the person already confirmed them, the questions still open, and the next setup step. Do not send secrets, credentials, customer rows, or end-user data.

name.description: The app or product name, for example from package.json or the README.

companyDescription.description: What the product does and who uses it, in a sentence or two.

context.description: What you learned about the app from the repo. Never include secrets or user data.

stack.description: Frameworks and services, for example Next.js, Supabase Auth.

appType.description: For example SaaS, marketplace, ecommerce, internal tool.

triggerTables.description: Tables whose new or changed rows could start emails, for example profiles or orders.

tools.name: get_database_role_setup
tools.title: Get database role setup
tools.description: Read-only. Use after the user agrees to database login setup. Returns transactional SQL from Dreamlit's shared role builder for a separate dreamlit_app login, with a password placeholder, grants summary, removal link and local setup instructions. For Postgres that isn't Supabase, including Neon, RDS, Railway and Render. Supabase apps use browser Supabase sign-in instead. Does not connect, run SQL or receive passwords. Lead with the setup page returned by get_setup_status: explain how Dreamlit uses the database, ask the person to connect there, and check get_setup_status when they say it is done. Optionally offer: "If you'd rather, I can connect it from here." Only if the person asks you to connect it does the following path apply. Before setting up a database login or calling connect_database, tell the user in a line or two, in plain words, how Dreamlit uses the database (Dreamlit works straight from the app's database, so it stays the source of truth: no syncing data to another tool and no tracking events to add. It reads the tables to know who should get each email and to fill it in with their real details, reacts as things change in the app (a new signup, an upgrade, a cancelled plan), and never changes the app's data. Nothing reaches users until they approve an email.) Then ask if you may set this up, in your own plain words. For Supabase (a supabase.co or pooler.supabase.com host, a Supabase MCP server or CLI, or an audit database note identifying Supabase), say: "To connect, you'll sign in to Supabase in your browser and pick this project. Dreamlit then sets up its own login that can read your tables but can't change your data. Want the link?" End your message with that question and wait for a yes in a later message, never in the same turn you ask. After that yes, call connect_database without a connection string and give the person the link; when they say it's done, call get_setup_status. Do not run get_database_role_setup or build or pass a Supabase connection string. Supabase sign-in is the supported path: it lets Dreamlit read auth.users and run Supabase Auth workflows. For Postgres that isn't Supabase (including Neon, RDS, Railway and Render), ask: "To connect, I'll create a separate database login for Dreamlit that can read your tables but can't change your data, and give Dreamlit only that login. Your own database password stays on this machine. OK to set that up on <host> / <database>?" End your message with that question and wait; create the login and connect only after they say yes in a later message, never in the same turn you ask. After that yes: get_database_role_setup → run its SQL locally → connect_database with the dreamlit_app connection string → get_setup_status. Get the table-owner role from SELECT current_user or the table owner. Generate a letters-and-digits password locally (for example openssl rand -hex 24), substitute [[REPLACE_WITH_PASSWORD]] locally, and run the transactional script with psql or your database MCP SQL tool using the access you already have. Build the limited connection string locally with username dreamlit_app and the same host, port and database. Never print the password or either connection string, or send the owner password to Dreamlit. If you can't run SQL, the host refuses CREATE ROLE, or the person declines the script, explain that in one line and offer either connecting with the app's own login after a second explicit yes or connect_database without a string for the browser link; never fall back silently. If connect_database returns usesLimitedRole=false, tell the person plainly: "Dreamlit is connected with your app's own database login." If its result includes a Supabase sign-in notice, relay it.

tools.title: Create or update workflow
tools.description: Creates a new Dreamlit workflow draft or updates an existing draft from an outcome-oriented natural-language prompt. tools.name: unpublish_workflow
tools.title: Unpublish workflow
tools.description: Use after explicit user intent to unpublish a Dreamlit workflow. Side effect: disables live triggers or schedules so no new runs start. Runs already in progress keep sending unless inProgressRuns is "stop". If the workflow has in-progress runs and inProgressRuns is omitted, returns clarification_required with the count and changes nothing: ask the user whether to stop those runs or let them finish, then call again with their choice. Returns updated workflow status, stopped run counts (allRunsStopped, remainingRunCount), and app URLs. If some runs could not be stopped, ask the user, then call again with inProgressRuns "stop": on an already-unpublished workflow it only stops the runs still in progress. Do not use for deleting drafts, canceling one broadcast run, or editing workflow content.

workflowId.description: Workflow id to unpublish and disable live triggers or schedules.

inProgressRuns.description: What happens to runs already in progress, including runs waiting at a wait step. "stop" stops them so they send nothing more; "let_finish" lets them keep going and send. Required when the workflow has in-progress runs: ask the user, then call again with their choice. On an already-unpublished workflow, "stop" stops the runs still in progress.
